says so. Credential values, URL userinfo and query strings never appear in logs, error messages
or telemetry.

#### Token expiry and the fallback model

lcg reads `ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN` once, at startup. A short-lived token that expires mid-run
surfaces as authentication failures (the gateway's response body is captured in the extraction
failure sidecar as for any non-2xx). If `LCG_EXTRACTION_LLM` names a `primary:fallback` pair, the
router treats such a failure as a primary failure and permanently switches to the fallback for the
rest of the process — but the fallback uses the same expired token, so it fails too. Use a
long-lived token, or an external refresher that restarts the process before expiry.

`lcg-eval` (the developer evaluation tool) does not honor these settings; its judge uses its own
fixed endpoint.

---

# Embedding Options

Source: https://docs.liminis.app/liminis-context-graph/embedding-options


**What should I run, on my platform, and what will it cost me?** This page answers that
question in one read. It is a capability matrix and a set of pointers, not a restatement of
the full reference — see [Configuration: Embedder sidecar](configuration.md#embedder-sidecar)
for every flag, environment variable, and resolution-order detail.

`liminis-context-graph` needs an external embedding backend reachable at startup. It talks to
that backend over the OpenAI-compatible `POST /v1/embeddings` contract, selected with either
`--embedder-uds <path>` (Unix domain socket) or `--embedder-http <url>` (HTTP).

## Capability matrix

| Option | Platform(s) | Install | Setup / model cost | Dimension | Flag | Offline? | Dimension auto-probe? | Unreachable at startup | Verification |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Swift CoreML sidecar** | macOS 26+ | Xcode command-line tools; build from [`native/local-inference/`](https://github.com/liminisapp/liminis-context-graph/tree/main/native/local-inference) | ~500 MB disk for the BGE-base-en-v1.5 CoreML model, downloaded on first setup; no per-call cost | 768 (fixed, BGE-base-en-v1.5) | `--embedder-uds` (or no flag — auto-detected at `/tmp/liminis-inference.sock`) | Yes, fully local | Yes | Fail-fast (socket-service mode) or bounded retry-and-degrade (`--mcp-stdio`) — see [Embedder sidecar](configuration.md#embedder-sidecar) | Verified — the [`swift test`](https://github.com/liminisapp/liminis-context-graph/blob/main/native/local-inference/README.md#tests) suite, and [`verify-embedding-parity.py`](https://github.com/liminisapp/liminis-context-graph/blob/main/native/local-inference/verify-embedding-parity.py) (cosine parity vs. the PyTorch reference, run manually — not yet wired into CI) |
| **Infinity** (Python, sentence-transformers-based) | Linux, macOS, Windows | Install and run [Infinity](https://github.com/michaelfeil/infinity) yourself; no download bundled with this repo | Depends on the model you load; Infinity itself is free/open-source, no per-call cost | Varies (model-chosen) | `--embedder-http` | Yes, fully local | Yes | Fail-fast or retry-and-degrade, same as above | Not independently verified in this repo — relies on the generic OpenAI-compatible contract. Listed as an unauthenticated-compatible server in [Configuration](configuration.md#http-transport-ci--linux--custom-embedders--hosted-providers) |
| **Ollama** | Linux, macOS, Windows | Install [Ollama](https://ollama.com), pull an embedding model (e.g. `nomic-embed-text`) | Model download only (varies by model, typically a few hundred MB); no per-call cost | Varies (model-chosen) | `--embedder-http` | Yes, fully local | Yes | Fail-fast or retry-and-degrade, same as above | Not independently verified in this repo — relies on the generic OpenAI-compatible contract. Listed with a concrete recipe in [Configuration: MCP client config recipes](configuration.md#mcp-client-config-recipes) |
| **vLLM / text-embeddings-inference (TEI)** | Linux (GPU recommended); macOS/Windows via Docker | Install vLLM or TEI, load a model | Model download (varies); no per-call cost; GPU strongly recommended for throughput | Varies (model-chosen) | `--embedder-http` | Yes, fully local | Yes | Fail-fast or retry-and-degrade, same as above | Not independently verified in this repo — relies on the generic OpenAI-compatible contract. Listed in [Configuration: MCP client config recipes](configuration.md#mcp-client-config-recipes) |
| **Hosted OpenAI-compatible provider** (e.g. OpenAI `/v1/embeddings`) | Any (network required) | An API key; no local install | No download; per-call pricing set by the provider | Model-chosen (e.g. 1536 for `text-embedding-3-small`) | `--embedder-http` + `LCG_EMBEDDING_API_KEY` (or `OPENAI_API_KEY`) | No — requires network | Yes | Fail-fast — an auth rejection (401/403) is always fatal and is **not** bypassable via `LCG_EMBEDDING_DIM` | OpenAI's own `/v1/embeddings` is **the concrete, verified case** — see [Configuration: HTTP transport](configuration.md#http-transport-ci--linux--custom-embedders--hosted-providers). Other self-described OpenAI-compatible hosted providers are not verified beyond this. |

Every non-macOS, non-OpenAI-hosted row above is caveated deliberately: none of them has been
run against a live instance and tested end-to-end in this repository. Their rows exist because
the wire contract they claim to speak matches what `OaiEmbedder` sends and expects — not
because this repo has executed an integration test against them. Treat that as "should work,
matches the documented shape," not "verified working here."

## Any OpenAI-compatible endpoint is a valid target

The rows above are examples, not an exhaustive list. **Any server that accepts
`POST /v1/embeddings` with an OpenAI-shaped `{input, model}` request and returns an
OpenAI-shaped `{data: [{embedding}]}` response is a valid `--embedder-http` target.** This is
the actual extension point — if your preferred embedding server speaks that contract, point
`--embedder-http` at it and it will work, whether or not it's named above. See
[ADR 0006](adr/0006-embedder-http-contract.md) and
[ADR 0016](adr/0016-oai-embedding-contract-uds-transport.md) for the wire contract itself.

## No bundled cross-platform option

If you are on Linux or Windows: **there is currently no bundled, zero-setup embedder for your
platform.** The Swift CoreML sidecar is macOS-only (it depends on CoreML and, for extraction,
Apple Foundation Models — neither exists on other platforms). You must run one of the external
options above (or any other OpenAI-compatible server) yourself and point
`liminis-context-graph` at it with `--embedder-http`.

This isn't an oversight: a native, in-process, cross-platform Rust embedder was evaluated and
rejected. See
[`docs/spikes/native-embedder-2026-05.md`](https://github.com/liminisapp/liminis-context-graph/blob/main/docs/spikes/native-embedder-2026-05.md)
for the full spike — `candle` was a **NO-GO**, `ort` was **GO-with-caveats**, and neither was
ever built into production. Out-of-process, over the same wire contract as every other row in
the matrix above, remains the supported path on every platform.

## Switching embedders on an existing workspace is not a drop-in swap

The embedding dimension is fixed into the graph's LadybugDB schema (`FLOAT[dim]`) at
database-creation time. `liminis-context-graph` auto-probes the dimension of whatever embedder
you configure at startup; `LCG_EMBEDDING_DIM` can override a **probe failure**, but it cannot
resolve a genuine mismatch between a newly-configured embedder's dimension and vectors already
stored under the old one.

If you switch to a different-dimension embedder against a workspace that already has content
in its `.lcg/` database, that is not something you can just reconfigure and restart into — see
[Configuration: Switching an existing workspace's embedder](configuration.md#switching-an-existing-workspaces-embedder)
for the remedy (full re-ingest, or `knowledge_recover` with `rebuild_from_workspace_wal`).

**Even a same-dimension model swap invalidates stored vectors.** Changing the embedding
*model* — even to one that happens to produce the same dimension — means your existing vectors
were computed by a different model and are no longer comparable to freshly-embedded ones.
Issue [#440](https://github.com/verveguy/liminis-context-graph/issues/440) added model-identity
stamping and mismatch detection for exactly this case (`knowledge_status`'s
`embedding_model_status` field, and the `embeddings_recompute_failed` /
`embeddings_recompute_skipped_no_text` counters, and per-group `zero_vector_rows` for rows left
with a zero vector by an embedder failure) — see
[Operations: `knowledge_status` health fields](operations.md#knowledge_status-health-fields)
for the full mechanics.

## Recommended instruction profile per embedder

Asymmetric models want a role prefix on queries (and sometimes documents). LCG adds it when you
select an [instruction profile](configuration.md#embedding-instruction-profiles); the default
`none` changes nothing.

| Embedder / model | Recommended `LCG_EMBEDDING_PROFILE` | Re-embed to adopt it on an existing workspace? |
|---|---|---|
| Ollama `nomic-embed-text` v1.5 | `nomic-v1.5` | **Yes** (document prefix) |
| e5 family | `e5` | **Yes** (document prefix) |
| Swift CoreML sidecar (BGE-base-en-v1.5) | `none` by default; `bge-v1.5` or `embedder` available | No (query instruction only) |
| Hosted OpenAI models, other symmetric models | `none` | n/a |

BGE's query instruction showed no clear gain on the v1 retrieval fixture (see the
[configuration note](configuration.md#does-the-bge-instruction-help)), so it is available but not
the default. LCG does not validate that a profile suits the configured model.

## Embedding is not extraction

This page is about **embedding** — the `--embedder-uds`/`--embedder-http` flags above. It has
nothing to do with **extraction**, the separate process of turning text into entities and
relationships, configured independently via
`--extractor-uds`/`--extractor-http`/`ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`. On macOS, the same sidecar process
can happen to serve both endpoints (`/v1/embeddings` for embedding, `/v1/chat/completions` for
extraction), which makes the two easy to conflate — but they are selected, resolved, and can
fail independently of each other. See
[Configuration: Extractor: local or hosted](configuration.md#extractor-local-or-hosted) for
full extraction configuration guidance.

## The macOS socket path is not shared with the Electron app

`liminis-context-graph`'s own default UDS auto-discovery path is
`/tmp/liminis-inference.sock` — a single, well-known, machine-wide path. The Electron
`liminis` app does **not** use that path: it launches its own sidecar process bound to a
separate, per-workspace socket at `<workspaceRoot>/.liminis/local-inference.sock`.

**These are two different sockets serving two different processes' sidecars — never one shared
socket.** A `liminis-context-graph` binary started by hand does not see, and cannot reach, the
sidecar the Electron app started for its own workspace, and vice versa. If you run a manual
CLI session alongside the app, expect to start (or point at) your own sidecar rather than
assuming the app's is reachable at the well-known path.

---

# IPC & MCP Reference

Source: https://docs.liminis.app/liminis-context-graph/ipc-mcp-reference


`liminis-context-graph` serves the same graph over **two transport surfaces**, both routed
through the same core dispatch in
[`crates/core/src/handlers.rs`](https://github.com/liminisapp/liminis-context-graph/blob/main/crates/core/src/handlers.rs) —
no graph logic is duplicated between them:

- **JSON-RPC 2.0 over a local socket** (default). Newline-delimited requests/responses over `.lcg/service.sock` — a Unix domain socket on macOS/Linux, a named pipe on Windows (see [Windows: named pipe](#windows-named-pipe)).
- **[Model Context Protocol](https://modelcontextprotocol.io) over stdin/stdout** (`--mcp-stdio`). Any MCP client — Claude Code, Claude Desktop, other agents — can query and mutate the graph directly.

### Windows: named pipe

On Windows the service serves the identical protocol over a named pipe, because `AF_UNIX` is not
usable from Rust's tokio, Node or CPython there (issue #581). `LCG_SOCKET_PATH` keeps its meaning —
it still names the workspace's endpoint — and maps to a pipe:

- **Discovery.** At bind the service writes the pipe name to `.lcg/service.endpoint` (the socket
  path with its extension replaced). Clients should read that file.
- **Name.** `\\.\pipe\lcg-<16 hex digits>`: FNV-1a 64-bit over the UTF-8 bytes of the absolute
  socket path, lower-cased, with `/` replaced by `\`. Stable per workspace, so a client that cannot
  read the file can compute it. A `LCG_SOCKET_PATH` (or `--connect`) that is already a
  `\\.\pipe\…` name is used as-is.
- **Access.** Only the user the service runs as (and SYSTEM) can connect; remote clients are
  refused, and a second process cannot bind the same pipe name.
- **Signals.** Closing the console, logoff/shutdown, Ctrl+Break and Ctrl+C all trigger the same
  graceful shutdown SIGTERM/SIGINT do on Unix.

A pipe opens like a file, so a client needs no socket library:

```python
import json
endpoint = open(".lcg/service.endpoint").read().strip()      # \\.\pipe\lcg-…
with open(endpoint, "r+b", buffering=0) as pipe:
    pipe.write((json.dumps({"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 1, "method": "health_check", "params": {}}) + "\n").encode())
    print(json.loads(pipe.readline()))
```

In Node, `net.createConnection(endpoint)` accepts the pipe name directly.

## IPC methods (60)

The socket dispatch handles **60 methods**: 59 `knowledge_*` methods plus `health_check`.
`health_check` is the one method not prefixed `knowledge_*`, and it is the reason the IPC
surface (60) and the MCP tool registry (59, below) differ by exactly one — `health_check` is
not exposed as an MCP tool. MCP clients have no health tool; the `ok` / `healthy` /
`ready_for_reads` semantics they would otherwise look for are in the
[Health check contract](#health-check-contract) below
([ADR-0855](adr/0855-health-check-ready-for-reads.md)).

| Category | Methods |
|----------|---------|
| Health | `health_check` |
| Capabilities | `knowledge_capabilities` |
| Status | `knowledge_status`, `knowledge_rebuild_status` |
| Ingestion | `knowledge_process_chunk`, `knowledge_process_document`, `knowledge_add_episode` |
| Document chunking (read-only) | `knowledge_preview_chunks` |
| Direct assertion | `knowledge_assert_entity`, `knowledge_assert_relationship` |
| Search | `knowledge_find_entities`, `knowledge_resolve_entity`, `knowledge_find_relationships`, `knowledge_search_passages`, `knowledge_query_cypher` |
| Typed walk (read-only) | `knowledge_get_ontology`, `knowledge_walk` |
| Graph reads | `knowledge_get_episodes`, `knowledge_get_nodes_by_group`, `knowledge_get_edges_by_group`, `knowledge_get_edges_by_uuids`, `knowledge_list_entities`, `knowledge_list_relationships`, `knowledge_get_entity_neighbors`, `knowledge_get_entities_by_source` |
| Correction reads | `knowledge_get_correction_changes`, `knowledge_get_affected_work` |
| Notebook health | `knowledge_lint` |
| Deletion | `knowledge_delete_episode`, `knowledge_delete_by_source`, `knowledge_delete_chunk_episode`, `knowledge_delete_by_group`, `knowledge_clear_all` |
| Supersession | `knowledge_mark_chunk_removed`, `knowledge_supersede_document`, `knowledge_retire_document` |
| Episode origin | `knowledge_stamp_origin` |
| Curation | `knowledge_merge_entities`, `knowledge_validate_corrections`, `knowledge_apply_corrections`, `knowledge_reprocess_entity_types` |
| Ontology | `knowledge_reload_ontology` |
| Relation typing | `knowledge_canonicalize_relations`, `knowledge_backfill_relation_types` (deprecated), `knowledge_reprocess_relation_types` |
| Semantic search maintenance | `knowledge_backfill_summary_embeddings`, `knowledge_reembed_missing` |
| Cross-group pointers | `knowledge_add_cross_group_edge`, `knowledge_rebind_pointers` |
| WAL administration | `knowledge_dump_wal`, `knowledge_strip_wal_embeddings`, `knowledge_prepare_checkpoint`, `knowledge_wal_mark_create`, `knowledge_wal_mark_list`, `knowledge_wal_mark_delete`, `knowledge_rebuild_from_wal`, `knowledge_build_indices` |
| Recovery / lifecycle | `knowledge_recover`, `knowledge_recover_full`, `knowledge_close` |

For request/response shapes and parameter details, the dispatch `match` arms in
[`handlers.rs`](https://github.com/liminisapp/liminis-context-graph/blob/main/crates/core/src/handlers.rs)
and their handler functions are the source of truth — this page is the method index, not a
copy of each handler's parameter parsing.

`knowledge_status` and `health_check` also carry an additive top-level `providers` object,
`{"embedder": "test" | "real", "extractor": "test" | "real" | "none"}` (#851), so a test can confirm
it is talking to the built-in providers started with `--embedder test` / `--extractor test`
rather than real ones; `"none"` means no extractor is configured. See
[Test Providers](test-providers.md).

`knowledge_status`'s WAL fields — including `wal.hydration_status` (issue #456), which
distinguishes a genuinely empty group from one whose WAL holds unapplied content — are documented
field-by-field in [Operations: `knowledge_status` health fields](operations.md#knowledge_status-health-fields)
rather than here.

**`knowledge_status` episode breakdown (issue #884, [ADR-0884](adr/0884-status-episode-breakdown-opt-in.md)).**
`knowledge_status` accepts an optional boolean `include_episode_breakdown` (default `false`; only a
literal `true` enables it). The feature is advertised as `status_episode_breakdown` by
`knowledge_capabilities`. It is opt-in because it scans every episode, `MENTIONS` edge and edge
while holding the read lock, which blocks writers for its duration; a call without it runs no extra
query and is unchanged. With it, the response gains:

```json
"episode_breakdown": {
  "as_of_us": 1763844000000000,
  "groups": [
    {"group_id": "g1", "live": 10, "superseded": 25, "pending": 0,
     "only_superseded_entities": 4, "only_superseded_edges": 7}
  ]
}
```

- `live` / `superseded` / `pending` partition a group's episodes. Liveness is the belief/search
  predicate (`EpisodeSupersession::live_at`) evaluated at `as_of_us`; `pending` is an uncommitted
  document revision (ADR-0785), never counted as live or superseded. Unattributed episodes are never
  superseded, so they are live. A future-dated supersession counts as live until its instant.
- `only_superseded_entities`: entities with at least one `MENTIONS` from a superseded episode and
  none from a live one (pending mentions are neutral). `only_superseded_edges`: edges whose belief
  state is `superseded` (every surviving producing episode superseded), counted by producer and not
  by fact text. Each is attributed to the entity's / edge's own `group_id` and counted once.
- Every field is present even at `0`; groups are sorted by `group_id`; the superseded : live ratio
  is `superseded / live`, computed by the client.
- When the database is not open, not queryable or the scan fails, `episode_breakdown` is `null` and
  `episode_breakdown_unavailable` is a reason string; the rest of the status response is unaffected.
- A workspace rebuilt from `knowledge_dump_wal` has no native `MENTIONS` (ADR-0828 finding F1), so
  `only_superseded_entities` reads `0` there.

Every long-running method above (the six WAL/recovery/reclassification operations most likely
to run for a while) accepts a `_progress_token` and streams `{"type":"progress",...}` frames
before the terminal result — see [Progress notifications](#progress-notifications) below.

### Readiness

A successful connection to `.lcg/service.sock` is **not** evidence the service is ready. The
socket is bound before the database opens — deliberately, so `health_check` and recovery IPC stay
reachable during degraded-mode recovery ([ADR-0009](adr/0009-degraded-mode-startup-recovery.md))
— and issue #378's WAL-root migration also runs in that same pre-open window, after the bind.
(Legacy `.graphiti/`→`.lcg/` workspace migration runs earlier still, before the socket is even
bound.) The process's own accept loop only starts once startup work has fully resolved, so a
request sent immediately after `connect()` queues in the kernel rather than racing the migration
with stale state — the real risk is a client that treats `connect()` succeeding as readiness by
itself and acts on that assumption (e.g. inspecting on-disk state) without waiting for a
`health_check` round-trip.

The correct readiness signal is a `health_check` round-trip reporting `"healthy"`:
`handle_health_check` only returns `healthy` once `Db::open()` has succeeded, which is after
migration has completed. Poll `health_check` until it reports `healthy` (or `knowledge_status`
until `connected` and `queryable` are both `true` and `initializing` is `false` —
`knowledge_status` has no `healthy` field of its own) before sending real work; see
[Operations: Self-healing and degraded mode](operations.md#self-healing-and-degraded-mode)
for the full rationale. A `degraded` response after startup has otherwise settled is a legitimate
outcome (e.g. unrecovered corruption) — not something to retry indefinitely.

A `busy` response (see [Health check contract](#health-check-contract)) is **not** a *write*
readiness signal: it means the service is alive but a write is holding or waiting for the write
lock — most importantly a long `knowledge_rebuild_from_wal`. Pollers that need to send writes keep
waiting on `busy` (gate on `result.healthy == true`) and must not treat it as failure. A client that
only reads gates on `result.ready_for_reads == true` instead, which stays `true` while `busy`.

### Capabilities

`knowledge_capabilities` (read scope; IPC and MCP; [ADR-0854](adr/0854-knowledge-capabilities-protocol-version-and-feature-registry.md), #854)
lets a client ask the running service what it is and what it supports. It takes no parameters
(unknown ones are ignored), reads no database and takes no lock, so it answers in degraded mode,
during a rebuild and under any `--writable-groups` policy.

```json
{"server_version": "0.19.1", "protocol_version": 1,
 "features": ["chunk_supersede", "entity_provenance", "episode_source_fields",
              "exact_source_match", "hybrid_passage_search", "implicit_default_group_warning",
              "lint", "origin", "passage_legs", "process_document", "ready_for_reads",
              "retire_document", "search_min_score_env", "status_episode_breakdown", "test_providers",
              "unchanged_noop", "walk", "walk_provenance", "writable_groups", "zero_vector_record"],
 "methods": ["health_check", "knowledge_add_episode", "…"]}
```

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `server_version` | The crate version, exactly as `--version` and MCP `initialize` report it (no `v` prefix; pre-release suffixes kept). |
| `protocol_version` | Integer, `1` today. Bumped **only** on a breaking change to the socket protocol (a removed or renamed method, a changed default scope or response semantics). A new method, field or feature does not bump it. Compare it for compatibility; do not infer features from it. |
| `features` | Sorted, duplicate-free `lower_snake_case` strings, one per capability. Append-only: a string is never renamed or removed once shipped. Test for the one you need; **ignore strings you do not recognise**. |
| `methods` | Sorted, duplicate-free names of every IPC method the dispatcher accepts, including `health_check` and `knowledge_capabilities`. It lists a method even if a particular call would currently be refused (degraded mode, write policy). |

**Old servers.** A server that predates this method answers `knowledge_capabilities` with its
ordinary unknown-method error: JSON-RPC code `-32000` and a message beginning `Method not found:`.
Treat that as "older than the capabilities method" and fall back to your own probing.

#### Feature strings

Every string in `features`, with the issue that introduced it. A string advertises that **this
build supports** the capability; it never reports run-time state (whether a mode is active, what
an operator configured) and does not promise a field is populated on every call. Strings added
by #885 name capabilities that shipped in 0.19.2 without one.

| Feature | Introduced | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `chunk_supersede` | closest known origin: #785 ([ADR-0292](adr/0292-chunk-ingest-never-supersedes-unattributed-episodes.md)); seeded by #854 | Chunk ingest can supersede earlier episodes of the same document. |
| `entity_provenance` | #857 ([ADR-0857](adr/0857-find-entities-episode-provenance.md)) | `knowledge_find_entities` can return episode provenance and filter by `uuids`. |
| `episode_source_fields` | #853 ([ADR-0853](adr/0853-episode-source-identity-and-exact-source-matching.md)) | Episodes carry stored `source_file` and `chunk_id`. Independent of `exact_source_match`. |
| `exact_source_match` | #853 ([ADR-0853](adr/0853-episode-source-identity-and-exact-source-matching.md)) | `knowledge_delete_by_source` matches the source exactly, with the safe legacy rule for episodes that predate stored source fields. |
| `hybrid_passage_search` | #789 ([ADR-0789](adr/0789-hybrid-passage-search-rrf-top-rank-bonus.md)) | Passage search offers the hybrid BM25 + vector mode. |
| `implicit_default_group_warning` | #856 | A write that omits `group_id` gets a `warnings` entry; pass an explicit `group_id` to avoid it. |
| `lint` | #755 ([ADR-0755](adr/0755-knowledge-lint-deterministic-health.md)) | `knowledge_lint` deterministic graph-health checks. |
| `origin` | #752 ([ADR-0752](adr/0752-episode-origin-and-corroboration.md)) | Episodes record an `origin`, distinguishing primary sources from corroboration. |
| `passage_legs` | #871 | Hybrid passage results carry `legs` (per-leg evidence). Present on hybrid results only; absent or null in other modes. |
| `process_document` | #785 | `knowledge_process_document` document mode. |
| `ready_for_reads` | #809, #855 ([ADR-0855](adr/0855-health-check-ready-for-reads.md)) | `health_check` carries `ready_for_reads`, present in every state. |
| `retire_document` | #859 ([ADR-0859](adr/0859-retire-document-and-orphan-reporting.md)) | `knowledge_retire_document` supersedes every live episode of a document with reason `document_removed`, deleting nothing. |
| `search_min_score_env` | #812 ([ADR-0812](adr/0812-search-min-score-env-default.md)) | The default passage-search `min_score` floor can be set by the operator with `LCG_SEARCH_MIN_SCORE`. The configured value is not exposed. |
| `status_episode_breakdown` | #884 ([ADR-0884](adr/0884-status-episode-breakdown-opt-in.md)) | `knowledge_status` can report a per-group live/superseded episode breakdown. |
| `test_providers` | #851 ([ADR-0851](adr/0851-test-providers-mode.md)) | This build supports the built-in deterministic `--embedder test` / `--extractor test` mode. It does not mean the mode is active; the active providers are visible in `providers`. |
| `unchanged_noop` | #858 ([ADR-0858](adr/0858-unchanged-chunk-resubmission-noop.md)) | Resubmitting an unchanged chunk is a no-op reported with status `unchanged`. |
| `walk` | #820 ([ADR-0820](adr/0820-caller-plans-walk-no-lcg-llm.md)) | `knowledge_walk` follows typed relations from an entity. |
| `walk_provenance` | #860 | `knowledge_walk` can include provenance episodes. |
| `writable_groups` | #742 ([ADR-0742](adr/0742-per-group-write-allow-list.md)) | The `--writable-groups` per-group write allow-list policy. |
| `zero_vector_record` | #808, #810 ([ADR-0808](adr/0808-replay-embed-retry-and-zero-vector-record.md)) | `knowledge_status` reports `wal_groups.<gid>.zero_vector_rows`, the record of rows stored with a zero vector. |

#### Changes deliberately not advertised

- **`knowledge_reembed_missing`** (#809, [ADR-0809](adr/0809-reembed-missing-zero-vectors.md), PR #826):
  a new method is already visible by membership in `methods`, so a string adds nothing. The status
  record it repairs has its own string, `zero_vector_record`.

### Health check contract

`health_check` never waits on the write lock, so it answers promptly even during a long WAL
rebuild ([ADR-0628](adr/0628-health-check-busy-state.md), #628). The response's `state` is one of:

| `state` | `ok` | `healthy` | `ready_for_reads` | Meaning | Supervisor action |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `healthy` | `true` | `true` | `true` | Alive and ready: DB open, no write in progress or pending. | Ready — send work. |
| `busy` | `true` | `false` | `true` | Alive, reads served, **not ready for writes**: a write is pending or in progress. | Alive — keep waiting for writes; reads may proceed; do not restart. |
| `degraded` | `false` | `false` | `false` | Alive but unusable: DB not loaded. `reason` says why. | Recover (`knowledge_recover`) or investigate. |
| *(no answer)* | — | — | — | Dead or wedged. | Restart. |

The three fields carry three different facts ([ADR-0855](adr/0855-health-check-ready-for-reads.md)):

- **`ok`** — liveness: the process is alive and answered. Gate on it for restart decisions.
- **`healthy`** — idle and ready for writes: DB loaded and no write pending or in progress. Gate on
  it before sending writes, or to wait for a rebuild to finish. It is **not** a liveness signal.
- **`ready_for_reads`** — reads are served now: the database is loaded. `true` while `busy`, `false`
  only when `degraded`. Gate on it before sending reads. It means "loaded", not "every read will
  succeed": indexes may still be rebuilding, and a read racing a mid-clear rebuild can fail.

Since ADR-0628 (0.16 era) `healthy` stopped meaning liveness. Raw-socket clients written before then
should use `ok` for liveness and `ready_for_reads` for read availability.

`busy` carries an `activity` field. While a `knowledge_rebuild_from_wal` job is running:

```json
{"ok": true, "healthy": false, "state": "busy", "ready_for_reads": true,
 "activity": "rebuilding", "job_id": "…",
 "progress": {"mutations_replayed": 48210, "wal_files_processed": 3,
              "wal_files_total": 12, "elapsed_seconds": 91.4}}
```

`progress` uses the same values as `knowledge_rebuild_status`. For any other writer the response
is `{"ok": true, "healthy": false, "state": "busy", "ready_for_reads": true, "activity": "writing"}`
with no `job_id` or `progress`. The busy path never connects to or queries the database.

Every `health_check` response, in every state, also carries `server_version` and
`protocol_version` (issue #854), with the same values as
[`knowledge_capabilities`](#capabilities). They are additive; no existing field changed.

Notes:

- `busy` means "a write is pending **or** in progress": a writer queued behind readers also makes
  the lock unavailable, so an otherwise idle service can briefly report `busy`.
- Batched passes ([ADR-0030](adr/0030-batched-write-lock-for-long-running-passes.md)) release the
  lock between batches, so during one the state alternates between `busy` and `healthy`.
- A streaming rebuild (`_progress_token`) is not registered as a job: it reports
  `activity: "writing"` without `progress`.
- Startup work (legacy and WAL-root migration, startup recovery) runs before the accept loop, so a
  probe sent then queues in the kernel and gets no answer until startup finishes.
- `healthy` can be reported in the short window after a rebuild job is registered but before it
  takes the write lock.
- `busy` has `healthy: false` on purpose: existing pollers that gate on `healthy` keep waiting.
  A liveness probe that only needs "is the process alive" should accept `ok: true`, and a read-only
  client should gate on `ready_for_reads: true`.

## Response contract (JSON Schemas, issue #852)

Method *names* are discoverable from the dispatch table; method *result shapes* used to be known
only from the code that built them, so consumers guessed key names. One such guess shipped a bug:
a notebook-health view read `knowledge_lint` details by the wrong keys (`details.derived_document`,
the `causes` map and `finding.reason` were each missed). lcg now publishes a
[JSON Schema (draft-07)](https://json-schema.org/draft-07/schema) for the result of each of these
methods, and its own test suite fails when a real response stops validating:

`health_check`, `knowledge_status` (including `wal` and `wal_groups`), `knowledge_search_passages`,
`knowledge_find_entities`, `knowledge_find_relationships`, `knowledge_process_chunk` and
`knowledge_lint` (with a per-category `details` shape, discriminated by `category`, and by `reason`
where one category has two shapes).

The schemas live in [`contract/`](https://github.com/liminisapp/liminis-context-graph/tree/main/contract)
as `<method>.schema.json` and are attached to every GitHub release, next to the binaries, together
with a `contract-manifest.json` that names the lcg version they belong to:

```json
{ "lcg_version": "0.19.1", "tag": "v0.19.1", "draft": "draft-07",
  "schemas": [ { "method": "knowledge_lint", "file": "knowledge_lint.schema.json", "sha256": "..." } ] }
```

**Fetch them at the version you pin**, exactly as you fetch the binary:

```sh
V=v0.19.1   # the lcg version you run
BASE=https://github.com/liminisapp/liminis-context-graph/releases/download/$V
curl -fsSLO $BASE/contract-manifest.json
for f in $(jq -r '.schemas[].file' contract-manifest.json); do curl -fsSLO "$BASE/$f"; done
```

**Validate a recorded response offline** with any draft-07 validator (no engine, no source
checkout). The schemas are self-contained: the only `$ref`s are internal (`#/definitions/...`).

```sh
# the recorded response is the JSON-RPC `result` value, saved to lint-result.json
npx ajv-cli validate -s knowledge_lint.schema.json -d lint-result.json
```

```python
import json, jsonschema   # pip install jsonschema
schema = json.load(open("knowledge_lint.schema.json"))
jsonschema.Draft7Validator(schema).validate(json.load(open("lint-result.json")))
```

**Generate types** from them with a stock generator, for example
`npx json-schema-to-typescript knowledge_lint.schema.json > knowledge-lint.d.ts` or
`quicktype -s schema knowledge_lint.schema.json -o knowledge_lint.rs`.

What the schemas say, and do not say:

- They describe a method's successful `result` only: not JSON-RPC error objects, `_progress_token`
  progress lines, or the MCP envelope (the MCP tools return the same result inside their own
  wrapper).
- A field that is always present is `required`. A field that is sometimes omitted is optional
  (`index_created_at` on an empty graph, `source_files` without `include_episodes`, `belief`
  without `believed_only` / `as_of`, `warning` on a normal `process_chunk`, `wal.scope` without a
  WAL root). A field that is always present but may be `null` is `required` and nullable
  (`derived_document`, `valid_at`, `embedding_cosine`, `next_cursor`).
- Alternatives are modelled as `oneOf` / `anyOf`: `health_check` by `state`, `knowledge_status`
  as degraded / queryable / not queryable, `knowledge_lint` findings by `category`.
- Free-form members stay loose on purpose (`attributes` is a JSON string, `rerank` / `expansion`
  are objects, `causes` is a map from cause to count), so they can grow without a breaking change.
- **Additional properties are allowed.** Validate with a stock validator and an unknown extra field
  still passes; do not turn on "additional properties: false" yourself unless you want every
  additive release to break you.

**Compatibility policy.** The schemas describe what lcg *emits*, so "breaking" is judged from the
reader's side. Removing or renaming a field, widening a type (`string` to `string|null`, `integer`
to `number`), making an always-present field optional, or adding an alternative to a `oneOf` /
`anyOf` is a **breaking change** to a published schema and is announced in the release notes as
such: a consumer that reads the old shape can crash or mis-parse the new one. Adding an optional
field, narrowing a type (`string|null` to `string`) or making an optional field always present is
not breaking: every response that validated against the new schema still validates for readers of
the old one. Every release that changes a schema lists the
change in the CHANGELOG. Contributors: see
[CONTRIBUTING.md](https://github.com/liminisapp/liminis-context-graph/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md#published-response-schemas).

## MCP-over-stdio transport

`liminis-context-graph --mcp-stdio` starts a native [Model Context Protocol](https://modelcontextprotocol.io)
server over stdin/stdout, using the official Rust SDK (`rmcp`). Any MCP client (Claude Code,
Claude Desktop, other agents) can query and mutate the knowledge graph directly — no Electron
app, no Node, no custom JSON-RPC client required. This is an *additional* external-facing
surface; the Unix-socket JSON-RPC protocol above is unchanged.

Every MCP tool is derived from the `knowledge_*` dispatch methods above — tool names match the
IPC method names verbatim, and each `tools/call` is translated into an `IpcRequest` and routed
straight through the same core dispatch the socket service uses. Tool descriptions and JSON
schemas are maintained in the
[`ToolSpec` registry in `crates/service/src/mcp/tools.rs`](https://github.com/liminisapp/liminis-context-graph/blob/main/crates/service/src/mcp/tools.rs) —
that file is the canonical source for per-tool descriptions; they are not duplicated here.

### Flags

| Flag | Description |
|------|-------------|
| `--mcp-stdio` | Starts the MCP server over stdin/stdout instead of binding the Unix socket. |
| `--scope=<list>` | Comma-separated list of scopes to advertise in `tools/list` (default `all`). See [Scopes](#scopes) below. |
| `--connect <path>` | Attached mode: forward every `tools/call` as JSON-RPC over the given Unix socket to an already-running service, instead of opening the database directly. By default the socket is dialled lazily, on the first `tools/call` — see [DB-access modes](#db-access-modes) below. |
| `--connect-eager` | Attached mode only: dial `--connect`'s socket at startup and exit immediately if it's unreachable, restoring the behavior attached mode had before issue #575. No effect without `--connect`. |
| `--allow-remote-close` | Attached mode only: advertise and allow `knowledge_close`, forwarding the shutdown to the remote service. No effect in standalone mode (no `--connect`). |

### DB-access modes

- **Standalone (default, no `--connect`)**: the MCP process opens the `.lcg` database directly,
  reusing the same startup and self-recovery path as the socket service ([ADR 0009](adr/0009-degraded-mode-startup-recovery.md)).
  Zero-dependency — works with no other process running.
- **Attached (`--connect <socket-path>`)**: the MCP process never opens the database; it
  forwards each call over the given socket to a service that already has it open. Use this to
  add MCP access to a workspace where another socket-service instance is already running,
  without contending for lbug's single-writer lock.
  - **Lazy connect by default (issue #575).** The socket is not dialled during startup —
    `initialize` and `tools/list` succeed immediately, serving the tool set from the compiled-in
    registry, regardless of whether the daemon at `--connect`'s path is up. The first
    `tools/call` triggers a dial; if it fails, that call returns a tool result with `isError:
    true` naming the socket path and suggesting you start the daemon, but the MCP process itself
    stays up and the client's session is unaffected — no protocol error, no exit. This avoids
    two failure modes a client can otherwise get stuck in for the client's own cached-failure
    window: registering a native MCP server before its daemon has started (first install,
    post-reboot), and the client caching a failed attach for several minutes even after the
    daemon comes up. Pass `--connect-eager` to restore the pre-#575 behavior of dialling at
    startup and exiting immediately (before `initialize`) if the socket is unreachable — useful
    if you rely on that fail-fast behavior as an external health check (e.g. a supervisor that
    restarts the front until the daemon is ready).
  - **Idle timeout.** `LCG_ATTACHED_CALL_TIMEOUT_MS` (default 30s) is a **per-read-line** idle
    timeout, not a whole-call timeout: it resets on every line read off the socket, including
    `{"type":"progress"}` lines. A call that keeps emitting progress is never bounded by it, no
    matter how long the call runs in total — only genuine silence (no output at all for the full
    timeout window) trips it. If the remote stops responding mid-call (e.g. it crashes), the
    attached client fails that call with a clean timeout error rather than blocking forever.
  - **Reconnect and retry.** If the connection to the remote breaks, the client transparently
    re-dials the same socket path rather than staying wedged. If the break is detected while
    writing the outgoing request — treated as safe to retry, since the write failing is the
    client's best available signal that the request didn't get through — the client
    automatically retries that request exactly once over the freshly-dialed connection. If the
    break is detected only after the request was fully written — while waiting for or reading
    the response — the call is **not** retried automatically, since the remote's execution
    status is unknown and blind retry could double-apply a non-idempotent write (e.g.
    `knowledge_add_episode`); that call fails with a clear "connection lost mid-call" error, but
    the connection is marked dead so the *next* call reconnects fresh. If a reconnect attempt
    itself fails (no listener at that path), the call fails with a clear, descriptive error —
    never a hang — and a later call will try reconnecting again. See
    [ADR-0040](adr/0040-attached-mode-reconnect-retry-boundary.md) for the full rationale.

### Scopes

Scopes are additive and composable (e.g. `--scope=read,admin`). `tools/list` advertises the
union of all active scopes.

| Scope | Methods |
|-------|---------|
| `read` | `knowledge_status`, `knowledge_capabilities`, `knowledge_find_entities`, `knowledge_resolve_entity`, `knowledge_find_relationships`, `knowledge_get_episodes`, `knowledge_get_nodes_by_group`, `knowledge_get_edges_by_group`, `knowledge_get_edges_by_uuids`, `knowledge_search_passages`, `knowledge_list_entities`, `knowledge_list_relationships`, `knowledge_get_entity_neighbors`, `knowledge_get_ontology`, `knowledge_walk`, `knowledge_get_entities_by_source`, `knowledge_rebuild_status`, `knowledge_validate_corrections`, `knowledge_get_correction_changes`, `knowledge_get_affected_work`, `knowledge_lint`, `knowledge_preview_chunks` |
| `write` | `knowledge_process_chunk`, `knowledge_process_document`, `knowledge_add_episode`, `knowledge_delete_episode`, `knowledge_delete_by_source`, `knowledge_delete_chunk_episode`, `knowledge_mark_chunk_removed`, `knowledge_supersede_document`, `knowledge_retire_document`, `knowledge_clear_all`, `knowledge_apply_corrections`, `knowledge_merge_entities`, `knowledge_reprocess_entity_types`, `knowledge_canonicalize_relations`, `knowledge_backfill_relation_types`, `knowledge_reprocess_relation_types`, `knowledge_add_cross_group_edge`, `knowledge_assert_entity`, `knowledge_assert_relationship` |
| `cypher` | `knowledge_query_cypher` |
| `admin` | `knowledge_dump_wal`, `knowledge_strip_wal_embeddings`, `knowledge_prepare_checkpoint`, `knowledge_wal_mark_create`, `knowledge_wal_mark_list`, `knowledge_wal_mark_delete`, `knowledge_rebuild_from_wal`, `knowledge_recover`, `knowledge_recover_full`, `knowledge_close`, `knowledge_build_indices`, `knowledge_rebind_pointers`, `knowledge_delete_by_group`, `knowledge_backfill_summary_embeddings`, `knowledge_reembed_missing`, `knowledge_reload_ontology`, `knowledge_stamp_origin` |
| `all` | every scope above (default) |

**`cypher` is a power scope, not bundled into anything else.** `knowledge_query_cypher` executes
raw Cypher with no param interpolation or value coercion — despite being a "query" method, it can
perform arbitrary mutations, and it bypasses the WAL-ordering and embedding invariants that the
structured write tools maintain. It is never implicitly included in `read`, `write`, or `admin`;
operators must opt in explicitly (or via `all`).

#### Per-group write allow-list

`--scope` decides which *tools* a connection sees; it does not limit *which groups* a
write-capable connection may change. When one daemon holds groups with different owners — say
layer groups hydrated from streams other parties publish, beside the group the local user
authors — start it with `--writable-groups=<g1,g2,…>` (or `LCG_WRITABLE_GROUPS`; see
[Configuration](configuration.md)). The list is enforced **inside the daemon**, at the one point
every request reaches, so it holds for the IPC socket (which has no scopes at all), standalone
`--mcp-stdio` and attached `--mcp-stdio --connect` alike. It is one list per daemon: there is no
per-client identity, and per-group *read* restriction is out of scope. Unset, nothing changes.

The check is made against the groups a call **actually changes**, not every group it mentions:

- An omitted (or `null`/non-string) `group_id` resolves to the default group, `liminis` — **the
  default group must be listed to stay writable.** `group_id: ""` is a distinct group that can
  never be listed, so it is always refused. A write that falls back to the default group also
  carries an [implicit default-group warning](#implicit-default-group-writes).
- `knowledge_add_cross_group_edge` is checked against the edge's own `group_id`. The
  `source_group_id` of a foreign endpoint is a read-only pointer and is not checked: with
  `--writable-groups=a`, `{group_id: "a", target: {source_group_id: "b", …}}` succeeds and
  `{group_id: "b", …}` is refused.
- A call that changes several groups needs **every** one listed, otherwise it is refused whole
  and nothing is written.
- The check runs before any handler work, so a refused call does no embedding or extraction and
  writes no database row and no WAL event. Reads of any group, and read-only tools, are never
  affected. `dry_run` gets no special case: a dry run on a non-listed group is refused too.
- Daemon-internal work — startup WAL replay, auto-heal index builds, degraded-mode recovery — is
  not a client request and is not blocked.

| Tool(s) | Group(s) that must be listed |
|---------|------------------------------|
| `knowledge_add_episode`, `knowledge_process_chunk`, `knowledge_process_document`, `knowledge_assert_entity`, `knowledge_assert_relationship`, `knowledge_merge_entities`, `knowledge_add_cross_group_edge`, `knowledge_reprocess_entity_types`, `knowledge_reprocess_relation_types` | `group_id` (default group if omitted) |
| `knowledge_supersede_document`, `knowledge_retire_document`, `knowledge_stamp_origin`, `knowledge_canonicalize_relations`, `knowledge_backfill_relation_types`, `knowledge_backfill_summary_embeddings`, `knowledge_reembed_missing`, `knowledge_reload_ontology` | the required `group_id` |
| `knowledge_delete_by_source`, `knowledge_delete_chunk_episode`, `knowledge_mark_chunk_removed` | every entry of `group_ids` |
| `knowledge_delete_episode` | the group that owns the episode (looked up; a missing episode is a no-op) |
| `knowledge_delete_by_group`, `knowledge_rebuild_from_wal` (every call, not just `force_clear`) | the target group(s) **and** every group owning a cross-group pointer row into them (ADR-0385: the purge/replay rebinds those rows) |
| `knowledge_rebind_pointers` | every group that owns a pointer row into `source_group_id` (those rows are what it rewrites; `source_group_id` itself is not written) |
| `knowledge_clear_all`, `knowledge_apply_corrections` | **every group present** (DB groups plus WAL directories). `apply_corrections` carries no group in its request and resolves names across all groups, so it fails closed |
| `knowledge_query_cypher` | refused entirely — see below |
| `knowledge_recover` | **while the database is degraded: exempt**, because a degraded database must stay recoverable ([ADR-0009](adr/0009-degraded-mode-startup-recovery.md)). **While it is healthy: every group present must be listed**, like `knowledge_clear_all`, because its strategies (`restore_from_backup`, `rebuild_from_workspace_wal`, `drop_lbug_wal`) replace or rewind every group's data |
| `knowledge_recover_full` | exempt: a no-op on a healthy database, and on a degraded one it only restores previously accepted state |
| `knowledge_strip_wal_embeddings`, `knowledge_build_indices`, `knowledge_prepare_checkpoint`, `knowledge_dump_wal`, `knowledge_wal_mark_*`, `knowledge_close` | exempt: they touch only WAL/checkpoint files, indices or process state, never group rows |

A consequence worth knowing: purging or rebuilding a listed group is refused while a non-listed
group still holds a pointer into it — list the owner too, or remove the pointer first.
(`force_clear` has been group-scoped since #378, not whole-database; only `knowledge_clear_all`
and `knowledge_recover`'s `rebuild_from_workspace_wal` span every group.)

**Raw Cypher is refused while a list is set.** `knowledge_query_cypher` cannot be scoped by group
— any statement can write anywhere — and the IPC socket and attached MCP have no scopes to turn
off, so the daemon refuses the method outright, reads included, with reason `raw_cypher_disabled`.
Use the structured `knowledge_*` read tools instead. It is refused rather than filtered because
no keyword scan can reliably tell a read from a write in Cypher (`CALL` procedures, `COPY`,
`LOAD`, `ALTER`, …). With the list unset, `cypher` scope is unchanged.

**Error shape.** A refused call fails with JSON-RPC code `-32004` and structured `data`; over MCP
the same object arrives as the tool error's `data`:

```json
{"code": -32004,
 "message": "knowledge_assert_entity refused: group 'b' not writable: not in --writable-groups (LCG_WRITABLE_GROUPS); writable groups: [a]",
 "data": {"reason": "group_not_writable", "group_ids": ["b"],
          "setting": "--writable-groups", "env": "LCG_WRITABLE_GROUPS",
          "writable_groups": ["a"]}}
```

`reason` is `group_not_writable`, `all_groups_required` (a whole-database operation with unlisted
groups present), `raw_cypher_disabled`, or `unclassified_method` (a method with no write
classification is refused rather than assumed safe). An attached MCP process cannot enforce the
list itself and rejects `--writable-groups` alongside `--connect`; set it on the daemon. See
[ADR-0742](adr/0742-per-group-write-allow-list.md).

**`knowledge_close` in attached mode is a footgun without `--allow-remote-close`.** In
**standalone** mode, `knowledge_close` is always advertised under `admin` scope and shuts down
only this MCP process's own DB connection. In **attached** mode, calling it would shut down the
*running remote service*. Without `--allow-remote-close`, `knowledge_close` is omitted from
`tools/list` entirely in attached mode (not merely rejected when called). Pass
`--allow-remote-close` only when you specifically intend this MCP connection to be able to stop
the remote service.

**Recovery and export live under `admin`.** `knowledge_rebuild_from_wal` (rebuild one group's data
from its own WAL directory — `group_id`, default `"liminis"`), `knowledge_dump_wal`
(snapshot/export the graph into a fresh compacted WAL directory), `knowledge_strip_wal_embeddings`
(rewrite existing WAL files in place to remove the embedding-vector `params` fields a pre-0.14
WAL still carries — see [Operations](operations.md#wal-administration)), `knowledge_wal_mark_create` /
`_list` / `_delete` (name a retained WAL position within one group's stream, without a full
snapshot — each also takes `group_id`, default `"liminis"`, and `_list` reports only that one
group's marks, never an aggregate across groups), and `knowledge_recover` / `knowledge_recover_full`
are all `admin`-scope tools — an attached client only sees them when launched with `--scope=admin`
(or `all`). If a mutation goes wrong, this is the recovery path. See [Operations](operations.md)
for the recovery model in full. Note the WAL replays **forward-only**, so take periodic
`knowledge_dump_wal` snapshots, or a lighter-weight `knowledge_wal_mark_create` named position, if
you want restore points before large or destructive operations — a mark does not survive
`knowledge_dump_wal`, since dump_wal renumbers sequence numbers and a copied mark's `seq` would be
meaningless against the new numbering.

**`knowledge_rebuild_from_wal` refuses to run against a non-empty group, unless you ask it not
to.** Since issue #378, one instance holds an independent WAL directory and applied position per
`group_id`; `knowledge_rebuild_from_wal {group_id, ...}` targets exactly one of them and never
disturbs another group's data or position. A `from_seq: 0` (default) full rebuild against a group
that already contains data fails fast with an explicit error rather than silently emitting a
duplicate-primary-key failure for every existing `Entity`/`Episodic`/`RelatesToNode_` row in that
group — the native write path uses `CREATE`, not `MERGE`, for those labels. Pass `force_clear:
true` to have the call clear *that group's* data automatically before replaying (the same
group-scoped purge `knowledge_delete_by_group` uses — this does **not** delete or reopen the
database file, unlike the pre-378 whole-database `force_clear` behavior), or clear it yourself
first with `knowledge_delete_by_group {group_ids: [group_id]}`. `dry_run: true` always fails fast
on a non-empty group regardless of `force_clear`, since a dry run must never mutate the database —
this lets a preview surface the problem before you commit to a real rebuild. None of this applies
to an incremental `from_seq > 0` resume, which intentionally targets a group that already has
state.

**Rebuild order across groups does not matter, and every rebuild reports `cross_group_rebind`
(issue #741).** A cross-group edge lives in the WAL of the group that *owns* it (say `layer`) but
points at an entity in another group (say `up`). Rebuilding `layer` before `up` used to leave that
edge permanently missing: its hop writes found no endpoint and did nothing, yet the pointer kept the
`bound` state cached in its WAL attributes. Now, after **every** successful rebuild — full or
incremental, reset-triggered or not, foreground or background job — the service (1) demotes any
`bound` pointer on an edge owned by the rebuilt group whose hop was not actually created to
`unbound` (local derived state, not written to any WAL), so `knowledge_status.cross_group_pointers`
reports the gap instead of claiming `bound`, and (2) runs the staleness-gated `rebind_pointers`
for pointers pointing *into* the rebuilt group, flushing each resulting mutation to the group that
owns the edge. Rebuilding `layer` then `up` therefore ends in the same graph as `up` then `layer`,
with no manual `knowledge_rebind_pointers` call. The result's `cross_group_rebind` carries the same
counts `knowledge_rebind_pointers` reports (zeros when nothing needed attention); it is `null` only
on a `dry_run`, or if the repair itself errored (logged, and the rebuild still succeeds).

**`to_seq` bounds replay from the other end: `from_seq <= seq <= to_seq`.** Pass an inclusive
upper bound to exclude a mutation (and everything after it) from a rebuild — e.g. a WAL-recorded
mutation that corrupted the graph. Omit `to_seq` for today's unbounded behavior (replay to the
end of the WAL); it must not be less than `from_seq`, or the call is rejected before any WAL line
is read or the database is touched. A bounded rebuild is **not durable**: WAL entries past
`to_seq` stay on disk, unapplied, not truncated or archived — a later unbounded rebuild, or a
`from_seq` resume that covers the excluded range, reapplies them, including a previously-excluded
bad mutation. `to_seq` bounds an endpoint; it does not add reverse/undo semantics to the
forward-only replay noted above.

### Search evidence and the similarity floor (`find_entities`, `find_relationships`)

Hybrid search fuses its candidate lists with Reciprocal Rank Fusion, which is rank-only: the top
hit of a gibberish query scores almost the same as the top hit of a perfect one, and every query
fills its top-k. To let a caller tell a real match from filler, each result of
`knowledge_find_entities` and `knowledge_find_relationships` carries an additive `search` object
(issue #629):

| Field | On | Meaning |
|-------|----|---------|
| `rrf_score` | both | fused, rank-based score — ordering only, **not** a relevance measure |
| `text_match` | both | `true` iff the full-text (BM25) path retrieved the item |
| `bm25_score` | both | raw BM25 score, or `null` |
| `name_similarity`, `summary_similarity` | entities | cosine similarity (`1 - distance`) on that vector path, or `null` |
| `fact_similarity` | relationships | cosine similarity (`1 - distance`) on the fact-vector path, or `null` |

A field is `null` when that retrieval path did not return the item (`text_match` is then `false`).
Values are raw and unnormalised; cosine similarity can be negative.

Both tools also accept an optional **`min_similarity`** (number). Vector candidates whose cosine
similarity is below it are dropped *before* fusion, independently per vector path, so they never
affect the ranking and are not reported for an item they did not qualify for. Full-text matches
always stay eligible, so an exact-name query still returns its match while a gibberish query
returns nothing. With the `kind` filter the floor applies on top of the kind path's bounded
nearest-neighbour probe.

How it differs from `knowledge_search_passages`' `min_score`: the value is clamped to 0–1 the same
way (a non-number is an invalid-params error), but `min_similarity` has **no default** — omitted
or `null` means no floor and results are identical to before, apart from the added `search`
object — and it acts before fusion and per path rather than as a post-filter on a single list.

### Entity provenance: which episodes mention an entity (issue #857, feature `entity_provenance`)

`EntityRow` carries `episode_uuids` and `source_descriptions`, but not every read fills them. Until
#857 the same field meant different things on different methods, so they are spelled out here:

| Method | `episode_uuids` / `source_descriptions` | `source_files` | Superseded episodes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `knowledge_find_entities` (default) | **Always `[]`** — not computed | absent | n/a |
| `knowledge_find_entities` with `include_episodes: true` | Filled | Filled | **Excluded** (live only; pending document revisions excluded too) |
| `knowledge_get_entity_neighbors` | Filled | absent | **Included** |
| `knowledge_get_entities_by_source` | Filled | absent | Included |

`knowledge_find_entities` takes an opt-in boolean **`include_episodes`** (default `false`; any
non-boolean is a validation error). Without it the response is byte-for-byte what it was before:
`episode_uuids` and `source_descriptions` are `[]` and no new keys appear. With it, each node's
fields come from the entity's **live** mentioning episodes — the belief/search predicate
(`EpisodeSupersession::live_at`) that `knowledge_walk` `include_provenance` also uses: not
superseded, not deleted, and not part of a document revision that is written but not yet
committed ([ADR-0785](adr/0785-document-mode-revisions-and-commit-boundary.md)), evaluated at the
read instant — computed from the single batched mention query that
already produces `support`, so there is no extra query per hit:

- `episode_uuids` — newest first (`created_at` descending, `uuid` descending as tiebreaker, the
  order `knowledge_get_episodes` uses), so a repeated call returns the same subset.
- `source_descriptions` — index-aligned with `episode_uuids`; not de-duplicated.
- `source_files` — the de-duplicated stored `source_file` values (#853) in order of first
  appearance. Episodes with no recorded source file (older data) are omitted, so this list is
  **not** index-aligned with `episode_uuids`. Present only with the flag.
- `episodes_truncated` — `true` only when the per-entity cap (fixed at **50**, not a request
  parameter) removed at least one live episode; absent otherwise. The cap is applied after the
  liveness filter, so excluded episodes never consume a slot.

An episode of a pending document revision is therefore absent until the revision commits, and
present afterwards — exactly as search and belief treat it. While a revision replaces an earlier
one, the earlier revision's episodes stay listed until the commit boundary.

**Caps differ on purpose.** `knowledge_walk` `include_provenance` returns at most **20** episodes
*per edge*, in the edge's recorded order, and always emits `episodes_truncated` (`false` when
nothing was cut). `find_entities` returns at most **50** *per entity*, newest first, and emits
`episodes_truncated` only when `true`. The units (edge vs. entity) and orderings differ, and an
entity is typically mentioned by far more episodes than an edge has producers, so a single value
would change shipped behaviour for one of them. Neither cap is request-tunable.

`support` and `corroboration` are unchanged by the flag and always count **every** live document
(live in the same sense as above, so a pending revision does not count), not just the capped
list; because `support` counts distinct documents and the list counts episodes, the two need not
agree. `get_entity_neighbors` and `get_entities_by_source` do not filter superseded episodes
(unchanged), so a `find_entities` hit's `episode_uuids` equals the **live subset** of what
`get_entity_neighbors` reports for the same entity.

To turn the UUIDs into episodes, call `knowledge_get_episodes` with `uuids` (see the paging
table below) — two calls from a free-text query to every mentioning episode.
See [ADR-0857](adr/0857-find-entities-episode-provenance.md).

### Hybrid passage search (`knowledge_search_passages`, issue #789)

`knowledge_search_passages` ranks episode passages in one of two modes, chosen per request with
`mode`:

| `mode` | Ranking | `score` | `similarity` |
|---|---|---|---|
| `vector` | Vector cosine, then belief-aware re-ranking by default (see `belief_aware`); with `belief_aware: false` it is cosine only, exactly the behaviour before #789. | Cosine similarity (`1 - distance`); a demoted passage's score is lowered to just below the passage it ranks under. | Not present. |
| `hybrid` | BM25 over episode text (the existing `episode_content` full-text index) and the vector ranking, fused with **weighted** Reciprocal Rank Fusion (`weight/(rank+60)` per list; the lexical list has weight 0.4, the vector list 1.0), then belief-aware re-ranking (see `belief_aware`). | The **fused rank score** (at most about 0.0233). It orders results; it is a rank-only fusion value, not a relevance, not a cosine and not comparable across queries. | Cosine similarity where the vector retriever matched the passage; absent for a passage only the lexical retriever found. **This is the relevance signal.** |

- **`mode`** is optional. Omitted, the service default applies: the `LCG_PASSAGE_SEARCH_MODE`
  environment variable (`vector` or `hybrid`; an unrecognised value warns on stderr and falls back
  to `vector`), else `vector`. An unknown or non-string `mode` is an invalid-params error. Callers
  that need plain cosine scores or a strict similarity floor should send `mode: "vector"` **and**
  `belief_aware: false` explicitly: `mode: "vector"` alone is belief-aware by default (since #806),
  which lowers a demoted passage's `score`. Sending both also makes them unaffected if the service
  default or `LCG_PASSAGE_BELIEF_AWARE` changes.
- **`belief_aware`** (boolean; default `true` in both modes since #806; omitted or `null` means
  "use the default"): after fusion and
  before truncating to `num_results`, two rules re-rank the candidate set (up to `3 × num_results`).
  A `derived` or `answer` passage that cites a `primary`/`external` note by `[[wikilink]]` (matched
  on that note's `doc_id`, within the same group) ranks below that note's best-ranked passage, so a
  page restating a fact does not outrank its source ([ADR-0752](adr/0752-episode-origin-and-corroboration.md)).
  A passage whose episode is no longer believed (a revision, or a superseded document;
  [ADR-0705](adr/0705-belief-time-separate-from-validity.md),
  [ADR-0707](adr/0707-document-supersession.md)) ranks below its successor. A rule applies only when
  the passage it ranks under is itself in the candidate set. A removed chunk has no successor and a
  document supersession with a future effective instant is still believed, so neither is demoted.
  Demoted passages are never dropped, and a demoted passage's `score` is lowered to just below the
  passage it ranks under, so **`score` can differ as well as the order**. In `vector` mode the same
  rules run on the vector ranking (`score` stays a cosine otherwise). `belief_aware: false` turns
  the rules off and returns, byte-for-byte, what the same request returned before #806 (cosine
  order and scores in `vector`; weighted RRF without the rules in `hybrid`). The workspace
  switch `LCG_PASSAGE_BELIEF_AWARE` (`off`, `0` or `false` disable; `on`, `1` or `true` enable;
  case-insensitive; anything else warns once on stderr and is ignored) sets the default for
  requests that omit `belief_aware`; an explicit request value always wins. With the switch off,
  `hybrid` gives weighted RRF without the rules, which is not the pre-#806 hybrid default (rules on).
  A non-boolean value is an invalid-params error. The removed `top_rank_bonus` parameter is ignored.
- **`legs`** and **`lexical_score`** (issue #871, additive, hybrid mode only): each hybrid passage
  carries `legs`, which retrievers found it: `dense` (vector only), `lexical` (BM25 only) or
  `both` (at any rank in each list). `dense` and `both` hold exactly when `similarity` is present,
  so `legs: "lexical"` is the documented form of the older "`similarity` is absent" convention.
  In single-query hybrid `lexical_score` is the raw BM25 value when the lexical leg matched, and is
  omitted otherwise. With `queries` (variants), `legs` is the **union** over every query that
  retrieved the passage (`dense` through one query plus `lexical` through another is `both`); the
  vector side counts only candidates at or above `min_score`. `lexical_score` is not set with
  `queries`, because BM25 values from different queries are not comparable. If the full-text
  index is unavailable, hybrid falls back to vector-only and every hit is `dense`. Both fields are
  omitted in `vector` mode, so a vector-mode response is unchanged. A passage that reached the
  result only through an `expand` HyDE variant (a vector-only search) carries no `legs`; a passage
  keeps the `legs` of the first stage list that returned it. `legs` does not change ranking,
  scores or membership.
- **`min_score`** (default `LCG_SEARCH_MIN_SCORE`, else 0.5; clamped 0–1) floors the *vector
  retriever's* cosine similarity before fusion, as `min_similarity` does for entity search. A
  passage found only by the lexical retriever is **not** excluded by it, so hybrid mode can still
  return hits for an off-topic query (E15: 25 of 34 off-topic queries, against 13 in `vector`
  mode); use `similarity` and `legs` to tell them apart. This is a deliberate change
  in meaning from `vector` mode, where `min_score` filters the single list. When a request omits
  `min_score` (or sends `null` or a non-number), the operator-configured default applies; an
  explicit number, including `0.0`, always wins. The effective default is reported by
  `knowledge_status` as `search_min_score_default` (additive, top-level, present in every status
  response shape). `LCG_SEARCH_MIN_SCORE` is validated once at startup: an empty, non-numeric, NaN
  or infinite value fails startup, and a finite out-of-range value is clamped to 0–1.
- **Fallbacks.** A query with no lexical tokens (punctuation or stop words only), or no lexical
  match, returns the vector ranking. If the episode full-text index is missing or inconsistent
  (for example right after an lbug upgrade, before the index is rebuilt) hybrid search silently
  falls back to vector-only, and the service logs one line on stderr per process. Query text is
  reduced to alphanumeric tokens before it reaches the index, so no query can cause a parse error.
- **Filters.** `group_ids` and `origins` ([ADR-0752](adr/0752-episode-origin-and-corroboration.md))
  are applied inside both the lexical and the vector query, so a passage excluded by either cannot
  enter through the other path.
- **Superseded episodes** are still returned in both modes; `belief_aware` only moves them below
  their successor.

The full-text index also covers an episode's `source` and `source_description`, so a query term in
a file name or description can match. Which mode is better is measured per category on the
retrieval eval (`lcg-passages` is the shipped default; `lcg-passages-raw`,
`lcg-passages-belief`, `lcg-passages-hybrid` and `lcg-passages-hybrid-belief` are opt-in; see
[retrieval-quality-evaluation.md](retrieval-quality-evaluation.md) and
[ADR-0789](adr/0789-hybrid-passage-search-rrf-top-rank-bonus.md)).

### Optional rerank and expansion stages on `knowledge_search_passages` (issue #796)

`knowledge_search_passages` accepts three **optional** parameters. Omit them all and the call behaves
exactly as before (same results, order, response shape and latency).

| Param | Type | Meaning |
|-------|------|---------|
| `rerank` | boolean | Rescore the top candidates with a local cross-encoder, blended with belief and recency. Overrides the workspace default (`LCG_RERANK`, default off). Latency (default model, Core ML, one maintainer machine): about 1.1 s p50 at 25 candidates and 1.9 s at 50 (the default), well over the 150 ms target; p95 not measured. The earlier ~587 ms figure was a Python/MPS run. See ADR-0796. |
| `rerank_candidates` | integer 1–50 | Candidates rescored (default 50, which is also the maximum; `LCG_RERANK_CANDIDATES`). Validated only when a stage runs (`rerank` / `expand` effective for the call), where a non-integer, negative or `null` value is an error; a call that runs no stage ignores it, so the default path is unchanged. An out-of-range integer is clamped to 1–50 and a warning is logged. Results beyond it follow in first-stage order, with no duplicates. |
| `expand` | boolean | Rewrite the query with a local LLM into lexical, semantic and hypothetical-answer variants and RRF-fuse their results (before rerank). Never a default; expected to cost on the order of a second (not yet measured). |

A non-boolean, non-null `rerank`/`expand` is an invalid-params error on every call, including one that would otherwise run no stage; omit the key or send `null` for "not specified". When a stage is requested the response
gains a block for it — `rerank: {applied, candidates, reason?, elapsed_ms?}` and/or
`expansion: {applied, variants, reason?, elapsed_ms?}` (`elapsed_ms` is the stage's wall-clock time, present
when the stage did work) — and the search **never fails** because a stage could not
run: it returns the un-staged results with `applied: false` and a `reason` (`not_configured`,
`unavailable`, `no_candidates`, `no_variants`). Each reranked passage gains `rerank_score` (cross-encoder
logit) and `belief` (`current` or `superseded`; omitted when unknown). `score` stays the first-stage
score (cosine in `vector` mode, the fused rank score in `hybrid` mode); only the order changes. The
first stage follows the call's `mode` and `belief_aware` (belief-aware is the default since #806; see above), except that a hypothetical-answer
expansion variant is always searched by vector. With `expand: true`, a passage the original query found
keeps the `score` computed against that query; a passage found only by an expansion variant carries that
variant's `score`, and `min_score` is applied to each variant's own query, so such a passage can have a
lower similarity to the user's query than `min_score`. `queries` (#802) compose with the stages: with `rerank` and/or `expand`, the user's own query runs the `queries` weighted-RRF pipeline as its first stage (LLM-expansion variants are single queries, searched as before), and the cross-encoder then reorders the fused result. The `belief_aware` ordering (a superseded passage
below its successor) is applied to each first-stage list, not to the fused result, so with `expand: true`
and **without** `rerank` it is not guaranteed; `expand: true` together with `rerank: true` ranks a
replacement above the note it supersedes when both are among the reranked candidates (`rerank_candidates`). See [Passage rerank and query expansion](configuration.md#passage-rerank-and-query-expansion).

### group_ids semantics: omitted vs. empty

Every read tool that accepts `group_ids` treats an **omitted or `null` `group_ids` uniformly as
"all groups"** (issue #413) — this holds across all 10 read tools: `knowledge_find_entities`,
`knowledge_find_relationships`, `knowledge_search_passages`, `knowledge_list_entities`,
`knowledge_list_relationships`, `knowledge_get_entity_neighbors`, `knowledge_get_entities_by_source`,
`knowledge_get_nodes_by_group`, `knowledge_get_edges_by_group`, `knowledge_get_episodes`.

**An explicit `group_ids: []` does not mean the same thing on every tool**, and this split is
deliberate, not an inconsistency to be fixed here:

- On `knowledge_find_entities`, `knowledge_find_relationships`, `knowledge_get_nodes_by_group`,
  and `knowledge_get_edges_by_group`, an explicit `group_ids: []` is preserved as "exactly these
  groups" — i.e. **zero rows**, a filter matching nothing.
- On the other six read tools (`knowledge_search_passages`, `knowledge_list_entities`,
  `knowledge_list_relationships`, `knowledge_get_entity_neighbors`,
  `knowledge_get_entities_by_source`, `knowledge_get_episodes`), an explicit `group_ids: []` collapses to the same
  behavior as omitting it — **all groups**.

If you need "zero rows" as a filter result, use one of the four tools in the first list, or check
the tool's own `ToolSpec` description in
[`crates/service/src/mcp/tools.rs`](https://github.com/liminisapp/liminis-context-graph/blob/main/crates/service/src/mcp/tools.rs)
before relying on `[]` to mean "nothing" — on the other six it doesn't.

This section is the single, central statement of that contract; individual tool entries on this
page don't restate it.

### Omitted-group behaviour per method (issue #856)

Many methods treat `group_id` as optional, and "omitted" does not mean the same thing everywhere:
writes fall back to the default group `liminis` (the Liminis app's own graph), most reads span
every group, and some methods refuse. **No default changed** with #856 — this table records what
each method already did. The classes:

- **default group + warning** — an omitted (or `null`/non-string) `group_id` resolves to `liminis`
  and the response carries an [implicit default-group warning](#implicit-default-group-writes).
- **default group** — an omitted group resolves to `liminis`, but the method is a read or an admin
  operation and gets no warning.
- **every group** — an omitted group means all groups.
- **refused** — the group is required; omitting it is an error.
- **not applicable** — the method takes no group (or is addressed by uuid / job id).

| Method | Omitted group means | Notes |
|--------|---------------------|-------|
| `health_check` | not applicable | takes no group |
| `knowledge_status` | not applicable | takes no group |
| `knowledge_capabilities` | not applicable | takes no group; returns the protocol version and feature registry |
| `knowledge_find_entities` | every group | `group_ids` omitted/`null` means all groups; see [group_ids semantics](#group_ids-semantics-omitted-vs-empty) for an explicit `[]` |
| `knowledge_resolve_entity` | default group | `group_id`; resolves by `(group_id, name)` in `liminis` only (read, no warning) |
| `knowledge_find_relationships` | every group | `group_ids` omitted/`null` means all groups; see [group_ids semantics](#group_ids-semantics-omitted-vs-empty) for an explicit `[]` |
| `knowledge_get_episodes` | every group | `group_ids` plus the legacy `group_id` alias are unioned; neither means all groups |
| `knowledge_lint` | every group | `group_ids` / legacy `group_id` scope; neither means all groups |
| `knowledge_get_nodes_by_group` | every group | `group_ids` omitted/`null` means all groups; see [group_ids semantics](#group_ids-semantics-omitted-vs-empty) for an explicit `[]` |
| `knowledge_get_edges_by_group` | every group | `group_ids` omitted/`null` means all groups; see [group_ids semantics](#group_ids-semantics-omitted-vs-empty) for an explicit `[]` |
| `knowledge_get_edges_by_uuids` | not applicable | addressed by edge `uuids`, not by group |
| `knowledge_get_correction_changes` | not applicable | addressed by episode uuid, not by group |
| `knowledge_get_affected_work` | not applicable | addressed by edge uuid, not by group |
| `knowledge_rebuild_status` | not applicable | addressed by `job_id` |
| `knowledge_search_passages` | every group | `group_ids` omitted/`null` means all groups; see [group_ids semantics](#group_ids-semantics-omitted-vs-empty) for an explicit `[]` |
| `knowledge_list_entities` | every group | `group_ids` omitted/`null` means all groups; see [group_ids semantics](#group_ids-semantics-omitted-vs-empty) for an explicit `[]` |
| `knowledge_list_relationships` | every group | `group_ids` omitted/`null` means all groups; see [group_ids semantics](#group_ids-semantics-omitted-vs-empty) for an explicit `[]` |
| `knowledge_get_entity_neighbors` | every group | `group_ids` omitted/`null` means all groups; see [group_ids semantics](#group_ids-semantics-omitted-vs-empty) for an explicit `[]` |
| `knowledge_get_ontology` | default group | `group_id` (blank also means default); read, no warning |
| `knowledge_walk` | default group | `group_ids` omitted means `["liminis"]`; read-style traversal, no warning |
| `knowledge_get_entities_by_source` | every group | `group_ids` omitted/`null` means all groups; see [group_ids semantics](#group_ids-semantics-omitted-vs-empty) for an explicit `[]` |
| `knowledge_validate_corrections` | not applicable | takes no group |
| `knowledge_preview_chunks` | not applicable | takes no group |
| `knowledge_add_episode` | default group + warning | `group_id`; write goes to `liminis` |
| `knowledge_process_chunk` | default group + warning | `group_id`; write goes to `liminis` |
| `knowledge_process_document` | default group + warning | `group_id`; write goes to `liminis` |
| `knowledge_assert_entity` | default group + warning | `group_id`; write goes to `liminis` |
| `knowledge_assert_relationship` | default group + warning | `group_id`; write goes to `liminis` |
| `knowledge_merge_entities` | default group + warning | `group_id`; write goes to `liminis` |
| `knowledge_add_cross_group_edge` | default group + warning | `group_id` is the edge's own group; `source_group_id` on an endpoint is a pointer, not a default |
| `knowledge_reprocess_entity_types` | default group + warning | `group_id`; write goes to `liminis` |
| `knowledge_reprocess_relation_types` | default group + warning | `group_id`; write goes to `liminis` |
| `knowledge_supersede_document` | refused | `group_id` is required; an omitted one is an error |
| `knowledge_retire_document` | refused | `group_id` is required; an omitted one is an error |
| `knowledge_stamp_origin` | refused | `group_id` is required; an omitted one is an error |
